caption: Table 5.1: Formulation of Cobalt(III) Chloride-Ammonia Complexes
note: text_layer null; read from the image. The table title is printed INSIDE target_box_in_crop, immediately above the header band, and is given in `caption`. The third header cell is printed over two physical lines ('Solution conductivity' / 'corresponds to') and is joined here with a single space. Notation: charges are printed as superscripts and formula counts as subscripts; both are flattened to plain characters, so the Formula cells read '[Co(NH3)6]3+3Cl-' for [Co(NH3)6] with superscript 3+ followed by full-size '3Cl' with superscript minus, '[CoCl(NH3)5]2+2Cl-' likewise, and '[CoCl2(NH3)4]+Cl-' for the complex cation with a superscript + followed by Cl with a superscript minus. The last two rows (Green and Violet) carry the same printed formula, as in the book -- they are the isomer pair the following paragraph discusses, not a transcription slip. Over-included by the crop and excluded as belonging to the body-text blocks: the paragraph above ('either chloride ions or ammonia molecules or both, remain bonded to the cobalt ion during the reaction and (ii) the compounds are formulated as shown in Table 5.1, where the atoms within the square brackets form a single entity which does not dissociate under the reaction conditions. Werner proposed the term secondary valence for the number of groups bound directly to the metal ion; in each of these examples the secondary valences are six.') and the paragraph below ('Note that the last two compounds in Table 5.1 have identical empirical formula, CoCl3.4NH3, but distinct properties. Such compounds are termed as isomers. Werner in 1898, propounded his theory of coordination compounds. The main postulates are:' followed by the start of '1. In coordination compounds metals show two types of linkages...'). The crop is clipped at the RIGHT edge; the title line and the third header cell both run to that edge but were confirmed complete at high zoom.
